common_name: Flamingo Queen Begonia (Large Silver-Spotted Cane Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cane cuttings or nursery starts after all frost danger has passed, siting in bright indirect light to partial shade; stake the canes early if a tall, upright specimen is wanted rather than a rounded mound.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained soil, allowing the top two inches to dry between waterings. Flamingo Queen carries large, medium-green cane-type leaves up to 12 inches long, marked with large silver spots and a thin silver edge along the margin. Left unstaked it forms a large rounded mound; staked, it can be trained upright to 3-4 feet. Bright pink flowers hang in large, showy clusters for much of the growing season. Recognized by the American Begonia Society in 2002, this cultivar prefers 40-60% humidity and is considered easy to grow for a large-leaved cane type.
sources: Steve's Leaves plant profile: Begonia 'Flamingo Queen'

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in a shaded spot after frost danger has passed; Taconite tolerates a wider temperature swing than most begonias and can summer outdoors in a shaded bed or container in mild climates.

directions: Grow in shade in well-drained soil, letting the mix go fairly dry between waterings. This compact shrub-type begonia, reaching only 10-12 inches, is grown chiefly for its dark, near-black foliage with a rich red reverse; under bright but indirect light the leaf surface flashes an iridescent royal blue, shifting through chocolate, copper, and bronze tones depending on the angle of light, an effect shared with iridescent species like Begonia pavonina. Taconite tolerates an unusually broad temperature range (roughly 20-95F) and lower humidity than most rhizomatous or cane types, and growers report it surviving outdoors as far north as USDA zone 7 with winter protection, making it one of the more cold-tolerant iridescent-leaf begonias in cultivation.
sources: American Begonia Society iridescent/shrub-type begonia references

common_name: Don Miller Begonia (Sandpaper-Textured Silvery-Blue Shrub Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed, in shade to partial sun; give it room to branch into a full, rounded specimen and stake the stems if a taller, 3-4 foot form is wanted.

directions: Grow in shade to partial sun in well-drained soil, letting the mix go slightly dry between waterings; this heat-tolerant shrub type branches readily into a full, rounded specimen about 2 feet tall (3-4 feet if staked). Bred in 1991 as a cross between the cane hybrid 'Torch' and the unidentified shrub species U062, Don Miller carries distinctive silvery-blue, sandpaper-textured leaves, and produces medium clusters of pink flowers in spring, summer, and fall that deepen to rosy red with more direct sun exposure. It is sometimes mistakenly sold under the name Begonia 'Frosty', a distinct plant, and shares seed-sibling parentage with the cultivar 'Maurice Amey'.

common_name: Pink Minx Begonia (Silver-Pink Splashed Cane Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cane cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed in bright, indirect light; pinch young plants to encourage branching, and provide higher humidity than most cane types since Pink Minx is prone to leaf drop in dry air.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained soil, watering when the top two inches of soil dry out and keeping humidity at 60 percent or higher. This compact cane-type begonia bears dark green, oval, pointed leaves with lobed margins, splashed and blotched with silver-pink; pinching young plants encourages a fuller, bushier habit. Small clusters of pink flowers appear over the growing season, with female blooms showing a rosy-red ovary behind pink petals. Because it demands more humidity than most angel-wing types, Pink Minx is best suited to a terrarium, greenhouse, or consistently humid windowsill rather than a dry interior room.

common_name: Red Fred Begonia (Maroon-Leaf Sport of Freddie Shrub Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed in shade to partial shade, and let the soil go fairly dry between waterings; give it room to spread into a large mounded shrub.

directions: Grow in shade to partial shade in well-drained soil, allowing it to dry fairly well between waterings; Red Fred forms a large, rounded mound 15-18 inches tall and wide. A sport of Begonia 'Freddie', it is distinguished by large, lustrous maroon oval leaves carried on light green stems covered in red scales. Tiny pink-and-red flowers rise in large clusters above the foliage in late winter and spring. Its vigorous, mounding growth and deep maroon color make it a strong textural and color contrast against green-leaved shade companions.

common_name: Lady Vanderwilt Begonia (Large Glossy Spotted-Leaf Cane Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cane cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed in bright, indirect light, staking the tall cane stems as the plant gains height.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in humus-rich, well-drained soil, watering when the top two inches of soil are dry. Lady Vanderwilt is an upright cane-type begonia reaching 3-4 feet, grown primarily for its large, glossy leaves boldly patterned with contrasting spotting across the leaf surface. Its scale and foliage impact make it a strong specimen or backdrop plant among shade-grown cane begonias such as Lucerna, though its outstanding feature is ornamental foliage rather than flowers. Keep humidity moderate to high and pinch young canes to encourage a fuller, multi-stemmed habit.

common_name: Maurice Amey Begonia (Metallic Pink Silver-Spotted Shrub Begonia)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after frost danger has passed in bright, indirect light with some direct sun tolerated; give this fast-growing shrub type room to branch into a large specimen.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with some direct sun in well-drained soil, letting the top two inches dry between waterings; this vigorous shrub-type begonia branches readily and reaches 2-3 feet tall. Bred in 1991 by Texas hybridizer Naron Stewart as a cross between the cane hybrid 'Torch' and the unidentified shrub species U062, and named for American Begonia Society member Maurice Amey, it carries large leaves in a bright metallic pink with faint silver spots and dark olive-green veins, backed by dark red undersides that develop a silver rim in good light. Small hanging clusters of bright pink flowers appear over the growing season. It shares seed-sibling parentage with the cultivar 'Don Miller'.
sources: Steve's Leaves plant profile: Begonia 'Maurice Amey'
